questions.q: Two friends stand at the pegs X and Y, 12 m apart. Each walks exactly 10 m, and they reach the same spot. How many such spots are there on the ground?
o: Two, one on each side of XY, both on the perpendicular bisector of XY
One, the midpoint of XY, since both friends walk the same distance
Infinitely many, since every point of the perpendicular bisector is equally far
None, since the 10 m walks are shorter than the 12 m between the pegs
questions.a: Two, one on each side of XY, both on the perpendicular bisector of XY

questions.q: O is the midpoint of XY, and A is a point such that angle AOX = 90 degrees. Show that AX = AY.
questions.a: OX = OY (O is the midpoint), angle AOX = angle AOY = 90 degrees (they form a straight angle with equal parts), and AO is common. So triangle AOX is congruent to triangle AOY by SAS and AX = AY.
s: States OX = OY and AO common
States angle AOY = 90 degrees as well
Concludes SAS congruence and AX = AY

questions.q: The midpoint of a straight road XY is O. A pole A stands 9 m from O on the north side and a pole D stands 7 m from O on the south side, and each pole is equally far from X and from Y. A wire is stretched straight from A to D. How long must it be?
o: 2 m
8 m

questions.q: Mira draws arcs of radius 7 cm from the pegs X and Y, which are 10 cm apart, and marks the meeting point A above XY. She then draws arcs of radius 12 cm from X and Y and marks the meeting point B, also above XY. She says, 'A and B are on the same side, so line AB cannot be the perpendicular bisector.' Which statement is correct?
o: AB is the perpendicular bisector, since A and B are each equally far from X and Y
AB is parallel to XY, since both points lie on the same side of the segment XY
AB bisects XY but is not perpendicular to it, since one point should lie on each side
AB cannot be drawn as a line, since the two radii 7 cm and 12 cm are different
questions.a: AB is the perpendicular bisector, since A and B are each equally far from X and Y

questions.q: A point T lies on the perpendicular bisector of XY, with TX = (2x + 3) cm and TY = (4x - 5) cm. (a) Form an equation and find x. (b) Find TX and TY.
questions.a: (a) T is equidistant from X and Y, so 2x + 3 = 4x - 5, giving 2x = 8 and x = 4. (b) TX = 2(4) + 3 = 11 cm and TY = 4(4) - 5 = 11 cm.
s: Part (a): equates the distances and gets x = 4
Part (b): TX = TY = 11 cm

questions.q: Arcs of the same radius are drawn from X and from Y, with XY = 10 cm, using radii 6 cm, 8 cm and 9 cm in turn. They give three points A6, A8 and A9 above XY. (a) What single line contains all three points, and why? (b) Sunil draws an arc of radius 8 cm from X and an arc of radius 9 cm from Y, and they meet at P. Is P on that line? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) The perpendicular bisector of XY, because each of the three points is the same distance from X as from Y. (b) No. PX = 8 cm and PY = 9 cm are unequal, so P is not equally far from X and Y.
s: Part (a): the perpendicular bisector of XY, since each point is equidistant from X and Y
Part (b): P is not on it because PX = 8 cm is not equal to PY = 9 cm

questions.q: True or False: A point that is 9 cm from X and 9 cm from Y, where XY is only 8 cm long, lies on the perpendicular bisector of XY. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. The point is the same distance from X and from Y, and every such point lies on the perpendicular bisector; it does not matter that 9 cm is longer than XY.
s: Verdict: states True
Reason: equal distance from X and Y puts the point on the perpendicular bisector, whatever the length of XY

questions.q: A leaf-shaped frame is made by joining the points AX, AY, BY and BX with wire, where AX = AY = BX = BY and the supporting line XY = 12 cm is not part of the frame. The wire used is 54 cm. The radius AX of the upper arc is ___ cm.

For sports day, the art club paints a leaf-shaped eye motif on a banner. The supporting line XY is 12 cm long. Anita chooses A above and B below with AX = AY = BX = BY = 8 cm. Rahul chooses C above with CX = CY = 10 cm and D below with DX = DY = 7 cm. The club has one string, 8 cm long, to use as its compass. (a) Does line AB pass through the midpoint of XY, and how far is the midpoint from X? (b) Does C lie on line AB, and why? (c) Will Rahul's eye be symmetrical about XY, and why? (d) The club wants Rahul's larger shape. Advise one change that keeps symmetry and say whether the 8 cm string can still be used.
questions.a: (a) Yes. AB is the perpendicular bisector, so it passes through the midpoint, 6 cm from X. (b) Yes. CX = CY, and XY has only one perpendicular bisector. (c) No, the upper radius is 10 cm and the lower is 7 cm, so CX is not DX. (d) Choose D with DX = DY = 10 cm too (it still lies on AB). The 8 cm string is too short for 10 cm arcs, so the club needs a longer string, or keeps Anita's symmetrical 8 cm eye.
s: Part (a): midpoint, 6 cm from X
Part (b): C lies on AB since CX = CY
Part (c): not symmetrical as CX is not equal to DX
Part (d): makes both radii 10 cm and notes the 8 cm string is too short

questions.q: Ravi draws the upper arc of an eye from A with AX = AY = 9 cm and the lower arc from B with BX = BY = 6 cm, on a supporting line XY of 8 cm. (a) Is the eye symmetrical about XY? Name the equality that fails. (b) He keeps A and redraws the lower arc to make the eye symmetrical. What must BX and BY be, and on which line does the new B lie?
questions.a: (a) No. For symmetry AX = BX is needed, but AX = 9 cm and BX = 6 cm. (b) BX = BY = 9 cm, and the new B lies on the perpendicular bisector of XY, the same line that holds A.
s: Part (a): not symmetrical because AX = 9 cm is not equal to BX = 6 cm
Part (b): BX = BY = 9 cm and B on the perpendicular bisector of XY, the line through A

questions.q: A and B are the centres of an eye on XY with AX = AY = BX = BY, and AB meets XY at O. Angle AXO is 62 degrees. (a) Find angle XAO. (b) Find angle XAY and angle AYX.
questions.a: (a) Angle AOX = 90 degrees, so angle XAO = 180 - 90 - 62 = 28 degrees. (b) AO bisects angle XAY, so angle XAY = 2 x 28 = 56 degrees; triangles AOX and AOY are congruent, so angle AYX = 62 degrees. Check: 56 + 62 + 62 = 180.
s: Part (a): angle AOX = 90 degrees, so angle XAO = 28 degrees
Part (b): angle XAY = 56 degrees and angle AYX = 62 degrees, checked by the angle sum

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Points A (above XY) and B (below XY) satisfy AX = AY = BX = BY, and line AB meets XY at O. Then angle XAO equals angle YAO.
Reason (R): Triangles ABX and ABY are congruent by SSS, since AX = AY, BX = BY and AB is common to both.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Points A and B are each equally far from the points X and Y, and line AB meets XY at O. Match each item in Column I with its value in Column II.
Column I: 1. length OX, if XY = 10 cm  2. angle AOX  3. angle XAO, if angle YAO = 34 degrees  4. length XY, if OX = (2t + 1) cm and t = 3
Column II: a. 14 cm  b. 34 degrees  c. 5 cm  d. 90 degrees

A segment XY is 18 cm long. Neel draws a line perpendicular to XY that cuts it 6 cm from X. Isha draws a line that cuts XY at its midpoint but makes 70 degrees with it. (a) Neither line is the perpendicular bisector. Give the reason for each. (b) By how far, and in which direction, must Neel move his line to make it the perpendicular bisector?
questions.a: (a) Neel's line is perpendicular but does not bisect XY, since it makes parts of 6 cm and 12 cm. Isha's line bisects XY but is not perpendicular, since the angle is 70 degrees, not 90. (b) The midpoint is 9 cm from X, so Neel must move his line 3 cm towards Y.
s: Part (a): Neel's line is perpendicular but cuts 6 cm and 12 cm; Isha's bisects but makes 70 degrees
Part (b): midpoint is 9 cm from X, so move 3 cm towards Y

questions.q: Priya draws A and B with AX = AY = BX = BY on a segment XY of 10 cm. With a protractor she finds angle AOX = 90 degrees and with a ruler OX = OY, where O is the point where AB meets XY. Her teacher says this does not yet show that AB is the perpendicular bisector for every segment and every radius. What does the congruence argument add?
o: It uses only AX = AY, BX = BY and the common side AB, so it holds for any XY and any radius
It measures the angles at O more exactly than a protractor can, so the 90 degrees is reliable
It shows the arcs must be drawn with a radius of exactly half of XY for the lines to meet
It shows AB is perpendicular to XY only when XY is 10 cm, as in her drawing
questions.a: It uses only AX = AY, BX = BY and the common side AB, so it holds for any XY and any radius

questions.q:
Statement 1: Any point that is 4 cm from X and 4 cm from Y, where XY = 6 cm, lies on the perpendicular bisector of XY.
Statement 2: Every point of the perpendicular bisector of XY is exactly as far from X as the midpoint of XY is.
Statement 3: A point moved along the perpendicular bisector, away from XY, stays equally far from X and from Y.
Which of the statements are correct?
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
questions.a: 1 and 3 only

questions.q: Show that a segment XY cannot have two different perpendicular bisectors.
questions.a: Both lines would pass through the midpoint O of XY and both would be at 90 degrees to XY at O. Only one line can be drawn at 90 degrees to XY through O, so the two lines must be the same line.
s: Notes both lines pass through the midpoint O
Notes both make 90 degrees with XY at O
Concludes only one such line exists so they coincide

questions.q: Two eyes are drawn on the same supporting line XY of length 8 cm. The first uses centres A and B with AX = AY = BX = BY = 5 cm. The second uses centres C and D with CX = CY = DX = DY = 9 cm. (a) On which line do A, B, C and D all lie, and why? (b) Which equality makes each eye symmetrical about XY? (c) Why do the two eyes still look different? (d) What condition on the common radius must hold for such an eye to exist on this XY? (e) How many different symmetrical eye shapes are possible on this XY?
questions.a: (a) On the perpendicular bisector of XY, since each point is the same distance from X and Y and XY has only one perpendicular bisector. (b) AX = BX, upper and lower radii equal. (c) The common radius is 5 cm in the first and 9 cm in the second, so the arcs curve differently. (d) The radius must be more than half of XY, i.e. more than 4 cm. (e) Infinitely many, one for each common radius greater than 4 cm.
s: Part (a): perpendicular bisector, equidistant points and only one bisector
Part (b): AX = BX
Part (c): different common radii change the curvature
Part (d): radius greater than 4 cm
Part (e): infinitely many, one per radius

questions.q: Meena and Imran live at M and I, 10 m apart on a lane. The panchayat will dig one well equally far from both houses. Three spots are surveyed. S1 is the midpoint of the lane, S2 is 12 m from each house, and S3 is 9 m from M and 11 m from I. Pipe costs ₹300 per metre to each house. Boring at S1 needs an extra ₹5,000 because the ground is rocky; S2 and S3 need no extra. (a) Which spots are equally far from both houses, and on which line do all such spots lie? (b) Find the pipe cost at S1 and at S2. (c) Find the total cost at S1 and at S2. (d) Which spot should the panchayat choose, and what does it show about the nearest spot?
questions.a: (a) S1 and S2 (5 m, 5 m and 12 m, 12 m); S3 is not (9 is not 11). All such spots lie on the perpendicular bisector of MI. (b) S1: 2 x 5 x 300 = ₹3,000. S2: 2 x 12 x 300 = ₹7,200. (c) S1: 3,000 + 5,000 = ₹8,000. S2: ₹7,200. (d) S2, cheaper by ₹800, though it is farther: the midpoint is the nearest equal spot but not the cheapest here.
s: Part (a): S1 and S2, on the perpendicular bisector
Part (b): pipe costs ₹3,000 and ₹7,200
Part (c): totals ₹8,000 and ₹7,200
Part (d): chooses S2 with the cost comparison

questions.q: Gita tries to prove that AB is the perpendicular bisector of XY, where AX = AY = BX = BY and AB meets XY at O. She writes: 'In triangles AOX and AOY, AX = AY, AO is common and angle AOX = angle AOY = 90 degrees because AB is perpendicular to XY. So by SAS the triangles are congruent and OX = OY.' (a) Which fact that she uses is the very thing to be proved? (b) Between which two sides must the equal angle lie for SAS to apply? (c) Which angle of triangle AOX must therefore be shown equal to its partner? (d) How can that be shown without assuming perpendicularity? (e) What then gives OX = OY and the two 90 degree angles?
questions.a: (a) That angle AOX = 90 degrees, i.e. that AB is perpendicular to XY. (b) Between AX and AO, so it is the angle XAO (not the angle at O) that SAS needs. (c) Angle XAO = angle YAO. (d) Triangles ABX and ABY are congruent by SSS (AX = AY, BX = BY, AB common), so angle XAB = angle YAB. (e) SAS on AOX and AOY gives OX = OY and angle AOX = angle AOY; these two angles form a straight angle of 180 degrees, so each is 90 degrees.
s: Part (a): she assumes the 90 degree angle, which is the conclusion
Part (b): the equal angle must lie between AX and AO
Part (c): angle XAO must equal angle YAO
Part (d): SSS on triangles ABX and ABY gives angle XAB = angle YAB
Part (e): SAS then gives OX = OY and equal angles at O, each 90 degrees

questions.q: Anil says, 'The perpendicular bisector is the only line that passes through the midpoint of XY.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: No. Infinitely many lines pass through the midpoint O of XY. Only one of them is also perpendicular to XY, and that one is the perpendicular bisector.
s: Gives the verdict that Anil is wrong
Says many lines pass through the midpoint
Says only one of them is perpendicular to XY

questions.q: At a temple, pegs stand at X and Y, 6 m apart, for the rope method. Three ropes are available: P of 8 m, Q of 10 m and R of 12 m between loops, costing ₹280, ₹300 and ₹340. Measurements show that with each rope the point A rises about 2.6 m, 4 m and 5.2 m above XY. The priest would like A at least 3 m above XY but says 2.6 m would still do for the seat, only 5 m of free ground lies above XY, and the trustees have ₹290 in hand. (a) For rope Q, how far is A from each peg? (b) Where does AB meet XY, measured from X? (c) Which ropes meet both the 3 m and the 5 m limits? (d) The trustees can buy P within their money, or ask for ₹10 more to buy Q. Which should they choose, and why?
questions.a: (a) 5 m from each peg, since the rope is folded in half. (b) 3 m from X, the midpoint of XY. (c) Only Q meets both limits: P gives 2.6 m, below 3 m, and R gives 5.2 m, above 5 m. (d) Either can be defended. Buying Q after finding the extra ₹10 meets the 3 m wish: that is about 3.4% over the money in hand (10 of 290), while P leaves the seat 0.4 m short of the 3 m need, about 13%. Buying P is defensible because the priest accepts 2.6 m and no extra money is needed. A justified choice that compares these earns the mark.
s: Part (a): 5 m from each peg
Part (b): 3 m from X, the midpoint
Part (c): only rope Q meets both limits
Part (d): chooses with the comparison of the ₹10 excess and the 0.4 m shortfall

questions.q:
Assertion (A): To draw a 90 degree angle at a point O on a line, one pair of arcs from X and Y is enough.
Reason (R): With OX = OY, the point O is itself one point of the perpendicular bisector of XY.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Dev must raise a right angle at a post O on a straight wall line using the rope method, with pegs X and Y placed the same distance from O on either side. Which setting lets him pull the rope midpoint off the wall line to a point A?
o: Pegs 3 m on either side of O, with an 8 m rope between the loops
Pegs 4 m on either side of O, with an 8 m rope between the loops
Pegs 5 m on either side of O, with a 9 m rope between the loops
Pegs 2 m on either side of O, with a 4 m rope between the loops
questions.a: Pegs 3 m on either side of O, with an 8 m rope between the loops

questions.q: XY is 10 cm. Arcs of radius 6 cm from X and from Y cross at A. Mohan says, 'A is on the perpendicular bisector, so it is 5 cm from X and 5 cm from Y, because half of 10 is 5.' (a) What are AX and AY really? (b) What does the 5 cm refer to?
questions.a: (a) AX = AY = 6 cm, the radius of the arcs. (b) The 5 cm is the distance OX = OY from the midpoint O to each end of XY, not the distance of A from them.
s: Part (a): AX = AY = 6 cm, the arc radius
Part (b): 5 cm is the distance of the midpoint O from X and from Y

questions.q: Gopal folds a rope so that one part is 4 m and the other 6 m, fastens its ends to pegs X and Y which are 8 m apart, and pulls the fold taut above XY to a point A. What can he say about A?
o: A is not on the perpendicular bisector of XY, since AX = 4 m and AY = 6 m are unequal
A is on the perpendicular bisector of XY, since both parts of the rope are fully stretched
A is on the perpendicular bisector of XY, since the rope is longer than the peg gap of 8 m
A is the midpoint of XY, since the two parts of the rope total 10 m
questions.a: A is not on the perpendicular bisector of XY, since AX = 4 m and AY = 6 m are unequal

questions.q: A student tries to construct the perpendicular bisector of XY = 10 cm. She draws arcs of radius 4 cm from X and Y above XY and arcs of radius 7 cm from X and Y below XY. (a) Do the upper arcs meet? Why? (b) Do the lower arcs meet? Why? (c) Can she join two points to get the bisector? What should she change? (d) With the change, where does AB meet XY? (e) What would still be a mistake if the 7 cm arc from X were replaced by 7 cm from X and 9 cm from Y?
questions.a: (a) No, 4 cm is less than half of XY (5 cm). (b) Yes, 7 cm is more than 5 cm. (c) No, she has only one meeting point. She should use a radius greater than 5 cm above (say 6 cm), or draw a second pair below. (d) At the midpoint, 5 cm from X. (e) The two arcs would not be equidistant from X and Y, so the meeting point would not lie on the perpendicular bisector.
s: Part (a): upper arcs fall short, 4 is under 5
Part (b): lower arcs meet, 7 is over 5
Part (c): only one point found, change the radius or add a pair
Part (d): meets XY at the midpoint, 5 cm from X
Part (e): unequal radii spoil equidistance

questions.q: Neha raises a 90 degree angle at O on a line, with OX = OY = 3 cm and the crossing point A. To check, she measures AX = 5.1 cm and AY = 5.1 cm. (a) What do the measurements AX = AY and OX = OY tell you about A and about O? (b) Does this show that angle AOX is 90 degrees? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Both A and O are equally far from X and from Y, so both lie on the perpendicular bisector of XY. (b) Yes. Two points of the perpendicular bisector fix the line AO, and that line is perpendicular to XY at O, so angle AOX = 90 degrees.
s: Part (a): A and O are each equidistant from X and Y, so both are on the perpendicular bisector
Part (b): line AO is that bisector, so it meets XY at 90 degrees

questions.q: Full circles with the same radius are drawn round the points X and Y, where XY = 8 cm. (a) How many points do the two circles have in common when the radius is 3 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm? (b) For the radius that gives a crossing, where do the common points lie?
questions.a: (a) With 3 cm: none, since 3 + 3 < 8 and the circles do not reach each other. With 4 cm: one, the circles touch at the midpoint of XY. With 6 cm: two. (b) The two common points lie one on each side of XY, on the perpendicular bisector of XY.
s: Part (a): 0 common points for 3 cm, 1 for 4 cm, 2 for 6 cm
Part (b): the two points are on the perpendicular bisector, one above and one below XY

questions.q: Compare the compass method and the rope method (Katyayana Sulbasutra) for the perpendicular bisector of a segment XY. (a) What plays the part of the equal radii in the rope method? (b) What plays the part of the pairs of arcs above and below? (c) Pegs are 6 m apart: what must be true of the rope length between the loops, and what happens with a 6 m rope? (d) What is the matching condition on the compass radius for a 6 cm segment? (e) Do the two methods give the same line, and why?
questions.a: (a) The two equal halves of the folded rope, fully stretched from the pegs. (b) The midpoint of the rope pulled above XY (point A) and below XY (point B). (c) The rope must be longer than 6 m. With a 6 m rope each half is 3 m, the rope lies along XY and its midpoint is the midpoint of XY, so no point off the line is found. (d) The radius must be more than half of 6 cm, i.e. more than 3 cm. (e) Yes, both find points equidistant from X and Y, which lie on the perpendicular bisector.
s: Part (a): the equal rope halves
Part (b): the rope midpoint pulled above and below
Part (c): rope longer than 6 m; a 6 m rope lies flat on XY
Part (d): radius more than 3 cm
Part (e): same line, both use equidistant points

questions.q: Kavita marks X and Y on a long bed edge 35 cm on either side of a point O, to raise a 90 degree corner at O with a string compass. She has strings of 36 cm, 50 cm and 80 cm. When tried, the arcs from X and Y cross at heights of about 8 cm, 36 cm and 72 cm above the edge respectively. Only 60 cm of free ground lies above the edge, and her teacher warns that arcs crossing at a very shallow angle make the crossing hard to read exactly. (a) What is the smallest whole-number radius that lets the arcs cross? (b) Does she need one pair or two pairs of arcs, and why? (c) Which strings give a crossing inside the free ground? (d) Which string should she use?
questions.a: (a) 36 cm, since the radius must be more than half of XY (half of 70 cm is 35 cm). (b) One pair, since O is already a point of the perpendicular bisector. (c) 36 cm and 50 cm; the 80 cm string crosses at 72 cm, beyond the 60 cm of ground. (d) The 50 cm string: the 36 cm string meets at 8 cm and crosses at a shallow angle, so the point is hard to read, while 50 cm crosses at 36 cm, clearly and within the ground.
s: Part (a): 36 cm, more than half of 70 cm
Part (b): one pair, because O is already on the bisector
Part (c): 36 cm and 50 cm only
Part (d): chooses 50 cm, balancing the shallow crossing and the space

questions.q: Make up a ground-marking situation for the rope method: pegs at X and Y 8 m apart. State one rope length (between the loops) that works, how far A then is from each peg, and one rope length that cannot give a point A off the line XY.
questions.a: With a 10 m rope, each half is 5 m, so AX = AY = 5 m and A is off the line XY. With an 8 m rope each half is 4 m, which only reaches the midpoint of XY, so A is on XY and not above it; a 6 m rope cannot even reach from X to Y.
s: A working rope length and AX = AY from the halves
A failing rope length with its reason
Links the halves to the 8 m gap between the pegs

questions.q: A long measuring tape lies along the ground. Pegs are fixed at the 2 m mark (X) and the 12 m mark (Y), and a 14 m rope is used for the rope method. At which tape reading does the line AB cross the tape?
o: 7 m
5 m
6 m
questions.a: 7 m

questions.q: Show that the perpendicular bisector of a 9 cm segment cannot be constructed using arcs of radius 3 cm from each end.
questions.a: The arcs from X reach points 3 cm from X, and those from Y reach points 3 cm from Y. Since X and Y are 9 cm apart, a point within 3 cm of X is at least 6 cm from Y, so the two arcs never meet and no point A is found.
s: States arcs reach only 3 cm from each end
Compares with 9 cm separation of X and Y
Concludes the arcs never meet

questions.q: A school marks 5 right-angle corners at points O1 to O5 on a track edge. For each corner, one arc centred at the corner cuts the edge at X and Y, and then one pair of arcs from X and Y gives the crossing point. A second school instead bisects 5 given segments, using two pairs of arcs each. (a) How many arcs does each school draw for one job? (b) How many arcs does each draw for all 5 jobs?
questions.a: (a) First school: 1 arc to mark X and Y, plus 2 arcs from X and Y = 3 arcs per corner. Second school: two pairs of arcs, 2 + 2 = 4 arcs per segment. (b) 5 x 3 = 15 arcs against 5 x 4 = 20 arcs.
s: Part (a): 3 arcs per corner against 4 arcs per segment
Part (b): 15 arcs against 20 arcs

questions.q: A mason has only a rope and pegs. He must mark a right angle at a post O on a straight line, with OX = OY = 3 m and an 8 m rope between its loops. (a) How can he place X and Y? (b) What does he do with the rope next, and which line gives the right angle?
questions.a: (a) Fix one end of the rope at O and swing it to cut the line at X and Y with OX = OY = 3 m, so O is the midpoint of XY. (b) Fasten the two loops to X and Y, fold the rope in half and pull its midpoint taut off the line to A. Then AO is the perpendicular bisector of XY, so angle AOX = 90 degrees.
s: Part (a): marks X and Y at equal distances from O on either side so O is the midpoint
Part (b): pulls the folded midpoint taut to A; AO is the perpendicular bisector, a right angle at O

questions.q: Pegs X and Y are 8 m apart. With ropes of 10 m, 12 m and 14 m between the loops, the rope midpoint pulled taut rises about 3 m, 4.5 m and 5.7 m above XY. Predicting from the rope method, what happens with an 8 m rope?
o: A does not rise: the rope lies along XY and A is the midpoint of XY
A rises about 1.5 m, continuing the steady fall in height as the rope gets shorter
A rises about 2 m, since the 8 m rope is the shortest of the four ropes
A rises about 6 m, since a shorter rope is pulled up more steeply
questions.a: A does not rise: the rope lies along XY and A is the midpoint of XY

questions.q: Ria raises a 90 degree angle at O on a line. She marks X 4 cm from O on the left, but by a slip marks Y 4.2 cm from O on the right, and then constructs the perpendicular bisector of XY. What does she get?
o: A line perpendicular to the given line, crossing it 0.1 cm to the right of O
A line through O that is tilted slightly from the perpendicular
A line perpendicular to the given line, crossing it 0.2 cm to the right of O
No line, since the arcs from X and Y cannot meet when OX is not equal to OY
questions.a: A line perpendicular to the given line, crossing it 0.1 cm to the right of O

questions.q: Priya says, 'In one pair of arcs, the arcs from X and Y must have equal radii, but the pair below XY may use a different radius from the pair above.' Is she right? Give a reason.
questions.a: Yes. A point that is the same distance from X and Y lies on the perpendicular bisector, so each pair needs equal radii within itself. Two such points, whatever their radii, fix the same line, so the pairs may differ.
s: Gives the verdict that Priya is right
Says equal radii within a pair give an equidistant point

questions.a: (a) 6 sides shared with the central cell and 6 shared between neighbours in the ring: 12. (b) 7 x 6 = 42 sides. (e) The six corners of the central cell, where three cells meet.
s: Part (a): 12 shared sides
Part (b): 42 sides in all
Part (c): 30 distinct sides, 90 cm
Part (d): 18 sides, 54 cm outer boundary
Part (e): 6 corners, those of the central cell
